review.notes: Taken to issue #11 depth (polygon, sector children, wave times, units, casualties, modern places). Sources read: English Wikipedia "Utah Beach" (rev. 1372907065) and "Normandy landings" (rev. 1386946425); Map VII of the official history Utah Beach to Cherbourg, read as the public-domain scan on Wikimedia Commons; Wikidata items for the present-day places; OSM data as served by OpenFreeMap tiles. The text of Utah Beach to Cherbourg and Cross-Channel Attack could not be read (history.army.mil 403 per #3; www.ibiblio.org, archive.org, www.openstreetmap.org, www.abmc.gov, www.utah-beach.com and fr.wikipedia.org refused by the session proxy), so every claim from the books Wikipedia cites (Balkoski 2005; Ford & Zaloga 2009; Whitmarsh 2009) is verified only as far as Wikipedia. Geometry derivation: Map VII of Utah Beach to Cherbourg (Commons scan, 1844x1142 px) has a 500-yard scale bar (163 px, so about 2.8 m per pixel) and a north arrow. On it, Uncle Red and Tare Green as established on D-Day meet at the Exit 2 road, Uncle Red running about 266 px (about 750 m) south of it and Tare Green about 263 px (about 740 m) north. As planned, Uncle Red ran from 424 px to 752 px and Tare Green from 752 px to 1122 px north of Exit 2. Exit 2 (Causeway 2, towards Sainte-Marie-du-Mont) was matched to the present-day D913, which meets the coast road at -1.17687, 49.4151; that point was projected onto the present-day OSM coastline and the map distances were laid off along the coastline from there. Seaward depth is the distance from the high-water mark to the low-water mark measured on Map VII at each sector boundary (about 0.8 to 1.4 km), applied perpendicular to the general line of the coast (bearing 319 degrees). Cross-check: Map VII's Exit 3 road, transformed the same way, falls within about 80 m of the point where the present-day D67 meets the coast. Accuracy is "approximate" because the 1944 map was georeferenced by hand from one road junction, a scale bar and the modern coastline, and the 1944 high- and low-water lines are not today's. Open questions: (1) Casualties: the issue asks for a range, but every readable source gives the same 197 for the 4th Infantry Division (Utah Beach and Normandy landings both cite Whitmarsh p. 51 and Ford & Zaloga p. 165), so no range and no "disputed" flag were recorded. Utah Beach to Cherbourg's own casualty count should be checked when its text can be read. (2) The Utah Beach infobox gives airborne casualties as "c. 2,499" while its text gives 2,500 (both Balkoski p. 331); 2,499 is also the Normandy landings article's count of American D-Day deaths, so the infobox figure may be a mix-up; the text figure is used. (3) The Wikipedia text calls the first-wave companies (B, C, E, F) "four companies from the 2nd Battalion" but then puts Companies A and D in the 1st Battalion; Map VII only labels them "Cos 8th Inf", so no battalion is given here for the first wave. (4) The wave times are from Wikipedia; Map VII gives the same schedule relative to H-Hour (H+5, H+15, H+17) but no clock time. (5) Left out: the Monument to the Fallen Danish Sailors (Wikidata Q108628151), whose Wikidata coordinate is about 2 km inland of the beach and could not be checked; the museum website (www.utah-beach.com, refused by the proxy).

summary.text: The westernmost of the five D-Day landing beaches, on the east coast of the Cotentin Peninsula west of the mouths of the Douve and Vire rivers. The US 4th Infantry Division, with the 70th Tank Battalion, made the seaborne assault; the 82nd and 101st Airborne Divisions had landed inland during the night to hold the causeways across the flooded ground behind the beach. The aim was to seal off the Cotentin Peninsula and take the port of Cherbourg quickly. The 8th Infantry Regiment landed first, in four waves from 06:30, on the beaches code-named Tare Green and Uncle Red. Strong currents set the craft down about 2,000 yards (1.8 km) south of the planned beaches, to a stretch near Exit 2 with only one strongpoint close by. Brigadier General Theodore Roosevelt Jr., the first senior officer ashore, decided to land the follow-up waves there rather than move the assault. Engineers and tank dozers cleared obstacles before the tide came in, the landing area was almost secure by 08:30, and the infantry then moved inland along the causeways to meet the airborne troops. German losses are unknown.
